questions.q: Under what specific condition does a Protected Custom Metadata Type actually hide its data from other users/orgs, per Salesforce's own Apex documentation?
options: Only when the org has Shield Platform Encryption enabled
Only when used within a managed package -- outside a package, it behaves exactly like a public custom metadata type
Protected Custom Metadata Types are always hidden regardless of packaging
Only when the user viewing it lacks the API Enabled permission
questions.explain: Salesforce's Apex reference is explicit that protected custom metadata types only behave as protected inside a managed package. Outside a package, they behave like public types, which are readable by every profile, including the guest user.

questions.q: In a typical, unpackaged org, what does this lesson say is the preferred home for most integration secrets used in callouts?
options: A plain custom setting
A string literal inside the relevant Apex class
Named Credentials, which manage callout authentication so the secret is never exposed to Apex code at all
A public custom metadata type
questions.explain: Named Credentials keep the secret off the Apex-visible path entirely for callouts -- this is the Salesforce-native answer this course has already built a full lesson around (Lesson 4).

questions.q: What is the documented fallback when Apex code genuinely needs to read a secret directly, rather than just handing a callout off to the platform?
options: A public custom metadata type
There is no fallback; this scenario is unsupported
A hardcoded constant in a utility class
An encrypted custom field, which stays encrypted at rest while still letting authorized Apex read it
questions.explain: For cases where Apex logic itself needs the secret value (such as computing an HMAC for webhook verification), an encrypted custom field is the documented option that keeps the value encrypted at rest.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does secret rotation matter even for a secret that's never been exposed?
options: Salesforce automatically invalidates any secret older than 90 days
Rotation is only necessary for secrets stored in a vault, never for Named Credentials
Risk accumulates over time regardless of known exposure -- more people/systems touch it, and an unrotated secret stays usable indefinitely if it's ever quietly exposed without detection
Rotation is purely a compliance formality with no real security benefit
questions.explain: A secret's risk grows the longer it goes unrotated, independent of whether anyone knows it's been misused -- 'we'll rotate if something goes wrong' already accepts an open-ended exposure window before anyone would know to act.

questions.q: What trade-off does this lesson describe for adopting a dedicated external secrets manager (vault) instead of relying on Salesforce-native storage alone?
options: A vault eliminates the need for any permission-set scoping on integration users
A vault is always strictly worse than Named Credentials with no benefit
A vault is required by Salesforce for any OAuth-based integration
A vault adds centralized rotation and auditing across platforms, at the cost of an extra integration hop and another system to operate and secure
questions.explain: A centralized vault is a legitimate architectural choice for a multi-platform secrets landscape, but it's a genuine trade-off -- more operational overhead and an extra hop -- not a strictly free upgrade over Named Credentials for a Salesforce-centric integration set.
